Stated Claim / Post Context:
Pala was almost 43 weeks pregnant when she gave birth. Her baby tragically died on delivery. As police investigate a family's very raw tragedy, a specialist says no doctor would let a pregnancy go that far

Police have launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of reality TV star Pala Negara's newborn son, following a delivery that came 20 days after his due date.

Actual Article Body:
By STEPHEN GIBBS, SENIOR NEWS REPORTER, AUSTRALIA and JONICA BRAY, SENIOR NEWS REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  09:53 AEDT, 30 October 2026   |  Updated:  09:55 AEDT, 30 October 2026

Australians have forgotten just how many mothers and babies died during childbirth before modern advances in medical care, according to one of the country's leading obstetricians.

Police have launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of model and reality TV star Pala Negara's newborn son, following a delivery that came 20 days after his due date.

The 38-year-old gave birth to a boy she called Harmony Hunter on August 28 at her home in Possum Creek in northern NSW after a pregnancy that lasted 42 weeks and five days.

Complications led to mother and baby being rushed to Lismore Hospital then transferred by a NeoRESQ helicopter to Gold Coast University Hospital where Harmony died less than 16 hours after his birth.

Negara, who appeared on Ex on the Beach: Couples in 2023, has said Harmony died of a brain injury caused by a lack of oxygen and restricted blood flow.

Associate Professor Gino Pecoraro from the University of Queensland could not comment specifically on Negara's pregnancy or Harmony's death.

But he spoke generally to the Daily Mail about the dangers of a prolonged pregnancy, which is usually defined as gestation which has continued beyond 42 weeks.

'The first thing to say is that absolutely no obstetrician would let a pregnancy go to 43 weeks,' Associate Professor Pecoraro said.

Police have launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of model and reality TV star Pala Negara's newborn son, following a delivery that came 20 days after his due date. Negara is pictured with her partner Chris Hunter

Negara gave birth to a boy she called Harmony Hunter on August 28 at her home in Possum Creek in northern NSW after a pregnancy that lasted 42 weeks and five days. She posted a series of pictures to Instagram after the loss of her son (above)

'I'm not aware of any obstetrician who would feel comfortable allowing a pregnancy to go that far if they were certain of their dates.

'Ten or 15 years ago, the magic number was 10 days after the due date based on a Canadian study, but in more recent times, most people would offer an induction of labour at 39 weeks.'

Professor Pecoraro, who is a past president of the National Association of Specialist Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, explained the risks of a prolonged pregnancy, also known as post-term or postdates.

'The baby outgrows the ability of the placenta to offer adequate nutrition and get rid of adequate waste products,' he said.

'If the baby's outgrown the ability of the placenta to support the baby, then it may not be able to tolerate the stresses of pregnancy.

'Unfortunately, placentas do age, and there does seem to be a use-by date.'

Asked why an expectant mother would choose not to be induced even if a baby was weeks overdue, Professor Pecoraro was blunt.

'This is a disease that we've got all around Australia at the moment,' he said.

Australians have forgotten just how many mothers and babies died during childbirth before modern advances in medical care, according to Associate Professor Gino Pecoraro (above)

'What's happened is that people forgot that mothers and babies used to die all the time. We're victims of our own success.

'Nowadays, people are only having one or two babies, and they want it to be an Instagram-worthy moment like the Kardashians.

'They think that you don't need obstetricians, that it's all natural and your body knows what to do.

'It is absolutely natural and one of the most natural things in the world but so is death in childbirth.'

Professor Pecoraro is a practising obstetrician and gynaecologist who reminds himself of the childbirth mortality rate of previous generations when he does regular locum work in regional Australia.

'One of the things I always do when I go to a new town is go to the cemetery,' he told the Daily Mail.

'And the number of times you see mothers and babies buried next to each other from you know 60, 100 years ago, is absolutely frightening.

'That's why the specialty of obstetrics developed because people were just tired of burying their women and babies.'

Professor Pecoraro said childbirth had become more 'medicalised' and most mothers gave birth in hospitals under expert supervision, rather than surrounded by family at home.

Former Ex on the Beach star Pala Negara announced the tragic death of her child in a social media post alongside her partner, Byron Bay hairdresser Chris Hunter, in September

'There are more tests that we do,' he said. 'Sometimes we do intervene and offer treatment. The trade-off for that is that you don't die.'

Negara announced the death of her baby in a social media post alongside her partner, Byron Bay hairdresser Chris Hunter, in September.

The Daily Mail revealed this week that officers attached to the Tweed and Byron Police District had commenced an investigation into Harmony's death and a report would be prepared for the coroner.

Speaking via telephone on Tuesday, Negara said she had been registered with a local home birth program provided through Byron Central Hospital.

Negara said she felt 'really let down with what happened with Harmony'.

'We did everything right,' she told the Daily Mail. 'We were under the Medicare system and I had my 41-week scan and everything was fine.'

In further correspondence via email, Negara said: 'At 41 weeks and six days, I was advised by text that care through the program would end because of its gestational limit'.

Harmony was born on August 28 at 4.27am and died in his parents' arms at 8pm.

Speaking via telephone on Tuesday, Negara (above) said she had been registered with a local home birth program provided through Byron Central Hospital

'I understand a rare silent placental abruption occurred during delivery and was identified only afterwards,' Negara said. 'Paramedics were called and, to my recollection, arrived approximately 40 minutes later.

'Harmony survived for 16 hours and passed away at Gold Coast University Hospital with the Queensland coroner's autopsy findings cause of death due to hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE).'

HIE is a brain injury caused by reduced oxygen (hypoxia) and restricted blood flow (ischaemia) to a newborn's brain before, during, or shortly after birth.

'Alongside our devastating grief, I am receiving counselling and recovering from postpartum haemorrhage,' Negara said.

'Harmony was deeply wanted and loved.

'He was the bridging of mine and Chris' families (from our previous relationships in which we each have two children) into one and our family deserves compassion and privacy. This was supposed to be our happy ending.'

In a series of photos shared on Instagram on September 7, Negara posed alongside her partner, and her two young children from a previous relationship, as she spoke of their loss.

'Creating life with the love of my life has been the most profound healing journey I could have never imagined being written into our journey,' she wrote in an Instagram post.

'Growing life for nearly ten months, growing our family, falling so deeply in love in a union that was always destined to be, falling in love with the life we have created for our family, birthing life, and then birthing death has been incomprehensible.

'My body feels broken and aches for our baby, the life we grew together. I don't think we will ever know how to move through this heartbreak.'
